To evaluate LifeStream's effectiveness, real-world datasets from fields like finance, physics, and biology were used, demonstrating improvements of up to 6 times in computation speed and 8 times in memory efficiency compared to the original code. When comparing LifeStream to hand-optimized numerical libraries, it showed comparable performance on synthetic benchmarks but significantly outperformed them on large real-world datasets, demonstrating the significance of data partitioning in memory-intensive applications.

We provide a precise definition of the Bertrand curve in three-dimensional Euclidean space and on a surface, as well as in higher-dimensional Euclidean space. We also examine the distinct types of the Bertrand curve in these contexts. Additionally, in three-dimensional Euclidean space, we outline the characteristics of a curve that satisfies the condition mentioned by Bertrand in an oblique manner.

Most neural network loss functions, including the popular Cross-Entropy loss, tend to favor overrepresented classes when data is imbalanced. This issue is particularly prevalent in NLP applications such as sentiment analysis and text classification, where loss functions that penalize the degree of belief reduction when moving from the positive class can yield superior results. Using the KL Divergence as an example, we demonstrate how this type of loss function can achieve performance comparable to CE when the class balance is even, and significantly outperforms CE when the classes are imbalanced. Furthermore, we find that a network trained with KD Divergence can provide a starting point for other, related tasks with little additional training, and that this approach can be interpreted as a degree-based softmax, which offers a mathematical explanation for its benefits.

This research focuses on developing a comprehensive thermomechanical model to simulate the crystallization of polymers resulting from deformation. To accurately capture this process, we utilize a combined thermodynamic and mechanistic approach that takes into account the interplay between chemical and physical changes occurring in polymer chains during crystallization. A unique feature of our model is its ability to account for different crystalline structures that can form within a polymer, including lamellar stacks and single crystals, through the application of a nucleation theory. Furthermore, we incorporate the impact of temperature and pressure on polymer crystallization. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our model, we conducted numerical simulations and compared the results to experimental data presented in the literature. Our model's predictions for the time-dependent crystallization, melting temperature, and crystalline structure development agree well with the available data.

The impact of complex Fermi surface topology on the magnetic susceptibility in superconducting materials is a previously unquantified effect. The simple approximation often used to calculate the Pauli parameter and magnetic susceptibility might be compromised in materials with a highly structured or disordered chemistry. Here, a first-principles approach is introduced to directly calculate the Pauli parameter from the electronic structure, without relying on the approximation. Utilizing this approach, the Pauli parameter of Sr$_2$YCl$_4$ is calculated as part of a study on the superconducting properties of this material. The method's applicability can be expanded to other materials and is particularly useful in assessing the sensitivity of materials to magnetic fields.

A conventional differential detection system is examined and its performance can be enhanced significantly. It is demonstrated that by utilizing the optimal threshold values, the error rate of a differential detected continuous phase modulation signal can be reduced substantially. In particular, for an ideal system with CPM, the error rate of differential detection can approach that of coherent detection. Furthermore, suitable threshold values are provided to enhance the performance of a non-ideal CPM system with differential detection. Additionally, the benefits of this technique are shown to be achievable over various channel conditions.

The thermodynamic properties of a system in constant pressure can be studied using the compressibility of the system. It has been proved that the validity of the grand canonical ensemble is linked to the specific condition that the root mean square fluctuation of the volume must be significantly large. In this study, we selected three different pairwise interacting gas models and employed the canonical ensemble to calculate their thermodynamic properties at high temperatures. We then used the pressure equation of state to investigate the compressibility of these models in various temperature ranges. Finally, we examined the validity of the grand canonical ensemble for each model based on their size-dependent thermal fluctuations.

To better understand complex sentences with implicit conditions, we need neural models to prioritize sentences with explicit prerequisites. Our research suggests that models can be made more effective by incorporating the hierarchical structure of if-then relation types. We discovered that models trained on a designated dataset for if-then relations could be further enhanced by being trained on a more comprehensive taxonomy of these relations. Our proposed framework addresses the challenge of automatically identifying the conditions expressed in each sentence. We further developed a novel approach to model sentence meanings as vectors that are then compared to determine the relation between sentences. Our approach also allows for incorporation of the proposed taxonomy into the comparison. Our findings show that both the manually curated and automatic data for if-then relations are beneficial for model performance. Our approach has potential applications in processing sentences with implicit conditions and can be used for modeling sentences with other types of implicit relationships.

The HHL algorithm's quantum superiority for matrix inversions is compromised due to its stringent accuracy requirements causing issues on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum machines.  To address this problem, we've developed the NISQ-HHL framework, a modified HHL algorithm tailored for these devices.  This framework's core idea is to divide complex matrices into simpler, approximate components and employs the quantum circuit's native averaging capability to enhance the accuracy of the inversions.  We've further established the relationship between HHL's original rotation operator and the approximate versions, demonstrating how the latter's accuracy directly results from the pre- and post-processing operations.  Additionally, we've explored ways to optimize the approximate implementations and executed the NISQ-HHL algorithm on a real quantum device, achieving a 6-fold improvement in its efficacy.  From our experiments, we've also derived a useful benchmark to assess the effectiveness of the approximate versions and include the code for the NISQ-HHL algorithm in the accompanying repository.

To enhance the connection between speech features and linguistic information, we propose the bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) for use in attention-based neural automated speech recognition systems. Speech attention and linguistic attention are both used to focus on crucial elements within the utterance and the linguistic structure, with the speech attention prioritizing components of the speech embedding and the linguistic attention prioritizing elements of the linguistic structure that best match the speech features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BiAM by incorporating it into a neural network-based ASR system and show that it surpasses a baseline system on the Switchboard dataset. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that BiAM generates meaningful linguistic attention that aligns with the syntactic structure of the sentence.

This research examines the number of initial reserved spaces in a parking lot, denoted as $P_n$, under the assumption that drivers base their parking decisions on positive integer-valued random variables following the Bernoulli distribution. The main focus is on analyzing the distribution of $P_n$ in relation to the total variation distance and Kolmogorov distance. As $n$ becomes large, we establish the convergence of the normalized first $k_n$ reserved spaces to a non-degenerate Poisson distribution, which provides an in-depth understanding of the distribution of the first $k_n$ reserved spaces and enables us to establish the asymptotic equivalence of total variation distance and Kolmogorov distance. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the normalized last $(k_n-n)/\log n$ reserved spaces to a non-degenerate binomial distribution, which sheds light on the last $(k_n-n)/\log n$ reserved spaces and reveals that the law of the last block can be found in the context of random apportionments.

Research on the physics of superconducting nanowires has expanded in recent years, with studies on the dynamics of voltage-controlled switching taking prominent stage. In particular, analyzing the nonlinear behavior of superconducting nanowires under an alternating voltage has yielded surprising results, revealing a switchable state that can be adjusted by changing the voltage, in both theory and practice. To better understand these findings, researchers developed a mathematical model that incorporates the effects of an applied voltage on the nonlinear dynamics of nanowires, and found it exhibited a switchable state with a critical voltage that can be changed by applying a bias voltage, both in the form of a step function and oscillatingally. Notably, when the bias voltage is in the form of a step function, the switchable state's barrier height can be adjusted by an order of magnitude, and when it's oscillating, the switchable state's barrier height also changes accordingly, suggesting that nonlinear dynamics of superconducting nanowires can be manipulated by changing the applied voltage.

Neural viewpoint-exchange networks, which generate images from novel viewpoints, can be constructed using a proposed framework that leverages dual generation models. This framework takes advantage of a pair of dual networks to produce images from novel viewpoints and incorporates an optimization process to ensure that the generated images match the original characteristics. Previous research used a single loss function to train both networks, but this limitation leads to insufficient exchange of viewpoint information. To address this challenge, a novel dual learning method is presented that utilizes two separate loss functions for the two networks, which are trained individually. This approach allows for a more effective exchange of viewpoint information and reduces the reliance on the optimization process. By applying this approach to two viewpoints, to novel views, and to 3D shape reconstruction, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing solutions.

A crucial component in quantum information systems is the beam splitter, and research has expanded the understanding of this concept to include higher-order photonic modes. By utilizing higher-order modes, a phase beam splitter can be designed to produce specific output phase relationships between input and output modes. The task at hand involves creating a device that directs a specific mode to a particular output, while rejecting others. The proposed higher-order mode beam splitter can be employed in a quantum protocol utilized for secure key distribution, and its performance has been demonstrated in a design utilizing single-mode optical fiber as the underlying structure. The results show that the device's effectiveness increases with the number of modes employed, ultimately leading to a higher success rate in implementing the beam splitter task. The proposed approach provides a versatile framework for designing a beam splitter that can be adapted to employ higher-order modes in a wide variety of underlying optical structures.

Using an approach that combines the principles of quantum mechanics and mathematics, we employ the Riemann-Hilbert problem to solve a complex integral equation originating from the interaction between two particles. We then apply this solution to analyze the resonance mass spectra of various baryon states. Similarity transformations are used to convert the interaction from a complex format to a real one, allowing us to interpret the results in the context of physical phenomena. We have conducted numerous tests to verify the stability of our approach and found that it successfully resists the breakdown caused by singularities within the analysis. Moreover, we have compared our method against other available approaches using the scattering amplitude. We have additionally explored different types of potential curves and demonstrated that the Riemann-Hilbert problem can be effectively extended to analyze such variations. We have also utilized our approach to re-examine the resonance mass spectra of certain baryon states and identified potential issues with previous findings. We have further utilized our approach to solve a complex integral equation that describes the interaction between three particles and has observed a unique phenomenon - where a certain particle state exhibits negative probability - we have also re-examined the resonance mass spectra of those baryon states and presented alternative solutions.

The spread of infectious aerosols in enclosed spaces is a significant transmission pathway for various diseases. To better understand this mechanism, we developed a 3D computational model that simulates the movement of tiny droplets carrying an infectious agent. To make the model more manageable and facilitate parameter sensitivity analysis, we simplified it into a two-dimensional model featuring a circular room with turbulent air flow. A comparative study using both models revealed that the simplified version accurately replicated the results of the more complex simulation, except in areas near the floor. When applied to a scenario involving a single infected individual in a large room, the simplified model showed that the aerosol concentration at the breathing level is lognormally distributed. When the models were used to predict aerosol concentration around the infected individual over time, the simplified model performed similarly to the more complex simulation, except in the initial period. When testing different room configurations and ventilation rates, the simplified model demonstrated its ability to accurately capture the effects of these variables on aerosol concentration.

This study investigates the impact of Bismuth layers on the Hall effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers through the Magneto-Seebeck effect and electrical transport measurements. Our findings indicate that the Hall effect is delayed by one layer of Bismuth compared to Cobalt layers, suggesting a different scattering mechanism for electrons. To understand this behavior, we used a model based on oxide surfaces to estimate the spin diffusion length in Cobalt, obtaining 0.46 nm. Furthermore, the data provide the layer-dependent resistivity of the Cobalt layers and allow for the estimation of the spin accumulation length in Cobalt layers as 0.93 nm.

This research investigates generalized versions of the N-dimensional Schr\"{o}dinger equation, incorporating fractional operators from Riesz and Hadamard, as well as a combination of both. The proposed models are applied to investigate the fractional Manning-Rosen potential. The formula for the fractional momentum operator is used, with a focus on analyzing the core potential's characteristics. The research utilizes the fractional approach to examine the eigenvalue problem in N dimensions. The results show that the fractional versions of the Manning-Rosen potential yield the same output as the classical version when N is 1, but in higher dimensions, the output differs. The paper also explores a fractional generalized Manning-Rosen potential and investigates the corresponding eigenvalue problem in N dimensions.

Deep neural networks have an uncontrolled Lipschitz constant when trained with standard loss functions, posing a significant security risk in sensitive applications. To mitigate this issue, Recent ADNE-L1 approaches attempt to establish a linear boundary for the network's output. However, the impact of these methods on network performance is poorly understood. In particular, it is unknown how selecting a $p$-norm affects the network's efficacy when training with a bounded Lipschitz constant. To address this query, we developed a neural network based on the $p$-norm, which includes the currently popular $l_1$ and $l_2$ norms as special cases. Our findings indicate that the $p$-norm-based approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art ADNE-L1 method, demonstrating that the choice of norm has a direct impact on both the network's performance and the tightness of its linear boundary. Notably, our research reveals that the optimal $p$-norm varies depending on the problem and can be used to adjust the network's performance in exchange for a tighter boundary. Our approach also allows us to create a neural network with a linear output space that is bounded by a sphere, which significantly reduces the size of the output space in comparison to a cube of the same volume. This presentation focuses on the development of an enhanced signal modeling approach for the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the LHC, building upon the existing NLO cross-section calculations for vector leptoquark signals. To mitigate limitations in current generator tools, the NLO$+$PS methodology is employed to integrate the higher-order corrections with parton-shower simulations. This methodology provides a more accurate model of the signal, accounting for variations in the number of final-state particles. By incorporating the ATLAS and CMS pile-up weights, the simulation is made compatible with the conditions of the experiments. To facilitate implementation, a dedicated VBF-NLO code repository has been established, featuring pre-integrated outputs suitable for use with the Pythia and Sherpa parton-shower and event generators. The utility is demonstrated through studies of vector leptoquark searches for $SU(2)$ and $U(1)$ charges, including scenarios with tau or charged lepton final states, where the findings are shown to align with previously published results from the ATLAS and CMS collaborations. The code is available upon request to interested research groups.

A novel deep-neural-network framework has been developed to enhance low-dose PET images by utilizing MRI images. This technique, named as DNN, employs two separate encoders to convert PET and MRI images into a combined feature map, which is then input into a decoder to produce a reconstructed PET image. The model was tested on 20 patients with brain cancer and 20 patients with lung cancer, resulting in improved image quality and quantitative performance compared to traditional reconstruction methods. Furthermore, it was found that utilizing MRI images for dose reduction in PET scans is feasible with DNN, resulting in a 4.0-fold increase in available scanning times or a 2.0-fold increase in reduced doses while maintaining similar image quality.

This study investigates the effect of contextualized language models on coreference resolution, specifically how they incorporate centering theory, by utilizing resources from the CoNLL coreference tasks. We observe that modern systems automatically achieve high accuracy without explicit theory application. To understand the impact of coreference resolution using contextualized embeddings, we retrain BERT on the data without patterns consistent with centering theory and find that it leads to artificial anomalies in the expected patterns of coreference. Furthermore, we determine that the issues result from incorrect assignment of labels for non-referring expressions rather than coreference itself. To rectify this, we propose a straightforward post-processing step that recovers the original accuracy of the coreferential relations by ensuring that non-referential labels are correctly assigned.

Enabling location-based services and efficient wireless networking relies on accurately determining the distance between WiFi access points and location fingerprints. Since the accuracy of distance estimation varies among machine learning predictors, it's essential to develop a robust approach. Prior research has primarily used simple distance metrics, which have limitations in capturing complex spatial information. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach, called Graph-Based Distance Estimation (GBDE), which leverages a graph convolutional network to estimate the distance between WiFi fingerprints by exploiting the topological structure of the radio signal propagation graph. The proposed GBDE framework utilizes a customized distance metric, perceives the environment through machine learning, and incorporates domain knowledge. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that GBDE significantly outperforms existing distance estimation methods and is robust in dynamic wireless environments.

As the demand for compact accelerators increases, Energy Recovery Linacs (ERLCs) are being considered more frequently.  To enhance efficiency, ERLCs employ a filling pattern where a high-current RF cavity is driven by a beam of charged particles.  Due to the interaction between the beam and the RF field, a threshold current exists, above which the RF cavity will be driven by the beam, leading to a loss of phase coherence and a failure to recover energy.  This research examines the impact of filling patterns on beam-RF interactions and identifies suitable design parameters to avoid a loss of phase coherence, ensuring the pulse-to-pulse energy recovery remains effective.  By analyzing the effects of filling patterns, we found that those with a large charge in the first pass can lead to an excessive beam-RF interaction, increasing the risk of a failure to recover energy.  On the other hand, filling patterns with a low initial energy can significantly reduce this risk, allowing the threshold current to be raised substantially.  By optimizing design parameters, it is possible to minimize the initial energy while maintaining adequate charge for a successful pulse-to-pulse energy recovery, thereby enhancing the reliability of ERLCs.

Using modern color orderings, the two-gluon contribution to the scattering operator's vertex in QCD was previously calculated by Low and Schwarz. This work extends those results to compute the three-gluon and four-gluon parts of the same vertex. Furthermore, building on a recent finding by Basso, Roehlig, and Trancanelli, it demonstrates that the two-gluon component of the vertex, after applying a specific transformation, matches the cusp anomaly in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory for six-gluon amplitudes. This extension also obtains the three-gluon and four-gluon components of the vertex, revealing they don't contribute to the cusp anomaly in the same way.

Researchers studied ideal polymer brushes on curved surfaces using a strong stretching small-scale model. They analyzed how surface curvature influences free energy, finding its expansion up to the fourth order in curvature. Additionally, they investigated Gaussian and parabolic surfaces, comparing their free energy to that of planar surfaces. For highly curved surfaces, a scaling analysis was conducted, revealing that the free energy depends on the square root of the surface's genus.

A graph G is considered to have a small metric dimension if it requires the fewest possible points to uniquely identify every other point via distance comparison. We investigate how the metric dimension of a truncated version of G changes in response to increasing the distance limit from 1 to d, and find that for distances up to d, the metric dimension of G is at most (2d+1) times that of the truncated version. We also examine cases where this ratio is much smaller. A notable example arises from the study of how the metric dimension of a Cartesian product G[X,Y] changes with increasing distance limits, showing that for distances up to d the metric dimension of G[X,Y] is at most (2d+1) times that of Y when X is a complete graph.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) exhibit complex variability across multiple timescales. Studying long-term variability is made challenging by the need to combine data sets originating from different observations, obtained over differing timescales through various telescopes. In this study, we addressed this issue by utilizing a novel stochastic simulation framework to model the time domains of AGNs, focusing on the $e$-folding time as the key parameter. We utilized an Markov chain Monte Carlo approach to estimate the distribution of $e$-folding times for individual objects. Our technique was applied to six quasars observed through different optical monitors in the ATLAS, yielding $e$-folding time estimates that vary from approximately 1 day to around 50 days for each quasar. Our study revealed nonlinear responses to illumination, along with an accumulation of short e-folding times in the distributions, which can be attributed to the variability of the radiation generated through electron-proton interactions.

The field of computing is concerned about whether approximately optimal solutions can be identified quickly, where "approximately optimal" is measured against a valuation based on a specific principle, such as the maximum matching in a graph or the most prominent flow in a network. This study examines the feasibility of an algorithm that, within a set number of steps, can produce a solution whose social value is no more than a fixed amount off from the optimal value, where the size of the deviation is relative to the optimal value. The possibility of creating such an algorithm is tested in four contexts: (a) finding the maximum matching in bipartite graphs where the valuation of each edge is a non-negative integer; (b) identifying the most prominent flow in a network where the valuation of each edge is a non-negative integer and there is a limited supply of items; (c) finding the maximum matching in bipartite graphs where the valuation of each edge can vary; (d) determining the most prominent flow in a network where the valuation of each edge can vary and there is an unlimited supply of items. The algorithm developed for each scenario includes a random start, generates a series of candidate solutions at random, and selects the solution that results in the highest social value, under the condition that the social value of each solution is calculated accurately. The algorithm's effectiveness is evaluated by assessing the likelihood that the selected solution is approximately optimal, where the likelihood is influenced by the maximum possible deviation, the size of the input, and the structure

The detection of small asteroids in wide-field surveys, such as Pan-STARRS1, is likely to produce thousands of unresolved objects. Using PSF analysis techniques, we can separate asteroids from comets by comparing the brightness of nearby background stars to a particular object's brightness. If the object appears significantly brighter than surrounding stars, it may indicate a small asteroid with a well-defined orbit. The most promising candidates will require verification through telescopic imaging or spectroscopy. The most reliable method for validating these candidates is by analyzing the shape of the point spread function, taking into consideration factors such as flat fielding, thermal noise, and charge-coupled device (CCD) bias. The best approach involves creating a finding chart for each candidate and photographing its surrounding area in detail. The most suitable targets for this approach will be asteroids detected over a relatively large area and those found at ecliptic latitudes between 4 and 20 degrees. The most likely comet-orbit candidates will then be identified from survey data and subsequently analyzed using the GPD method.

This study undertakes a comprehensive examination of network peer effects by incorporating individual-specific influences from multiple dimensions. We begin by reviewing the existing empirical research on network peer effects, discussing various challenges and approaches for analyzing these effects. Next, we outline a new empirical strategy that leverages structural equation modeling to investigate the impact of network influences on an individual's behavior. This method allows us to estimate the effects of specific peers or network groups on individual outcomes. To apply and test our approach, we analyze a unique data set comprising information about friendships, social interactions, and academic performance for 360 college students. Using this data, we develop and evaluate several models that incorporate the effects of network influences on academic outcomes. Our results indicate that the presence of certain peers can either positively or negatively influence a student's academic performance. We also find that the impact of a peer's major on a student's outcome is mediated by social interactions, whereas the impact of a peer's ethnicity is not. Furthermore, we show that the method can accurately estimate the effects of a network group on individual outcomes, and that these effects are meaningful when compared to traditional approaches.

This study develops multiple chain rule formulas for the variable-order Riemann-Liouville and the variable-order Caputo fractional derivatives and integrals. Initially, we establish fundamental formulae for these operators through a direct application of their defining equations. Subsequently, several chain rule formulas are derived utilizing different methods. Notably, we utilize these formulas to demonstrate their equivalence in specific contexts. Moreover, we illustrate the scope and limitations of these formulas by examining a sample fractional differential equation.

In our study, we incorporated a theory-of-mind approach into a collaborative game to examine if taking another player's perspective would lead to greater success in achieving individual goals. Theoretical background suggested that incorporating another player's mental states could provide a deeper understanding of their behavior, facilitating the achievement of individual goals. However, our findings indicated that considering another player's perspective, although beneficial in some cases, did not always lead to greater success in achieving individual goals. In fact, in most situations, it had the opposite effect. The data also revealed that players who successfully achieved their goals did not consider their partner's thoughts and intentions. This was particularly true when the partner's actions were already well understood through observation of the game's state. The research's limitations are discussed, along with potential areas for further exploration.

Comparing the intricate folding pathways of knotted proteins to those without knots is a compelling challenge. Recent studies have made significant headway in reconstructing these pathways for a few selected proteins. In this work, we apply a similar approach to determine the most likely sequence of events in the folding process of three shallot knotted proteins, along with four deeply knotted proteins, by using molecular dynamics simulations and comparison with native structures. A key observation stands out - the formation of a knot occurs after the initial folding phase in shallot knotted proteins, in contrast to deeply knotted proteins where the knot folds almost simultaneously with the chain. Our data also reveal that the folding pathways of shallot knotted proteins differ significantly from those of deeply knotted proteins, with multiple possible routes to knot formation evident in the former. A preliminary analysis suggests that factors such as secondary structure patterns and hydrophobic interactions play a crucial role in determining the folding pathways of these proteins. A more in-depth examination of the same factors in nature-based sequences shows that the underlying biology holds the key to understanding and predicting the intricate folding mechanisms of knotted proteins.

Given a connected, orientable surface $S$ and a symplectic form $\omega$ on the product $P\times S$, we examine the condition of irrationality, asking that $\omega$ not be expressible as a sum of $\omega_P$ and a function of $H_2(P\times S)$. For a vast class of closed, oriented manifolds $P$ with surfaces as factors, we demonstrate that this irrationality condition can be equivalently defined using topological characteristics. Specifically, for $P$ possessing a symplectic form $\omega_P$ with specified properties and a non-trivial first homology group $H_1(P)\neq 0$, we show that the irrationality of $\omega$ relies solely on the topological properties of $P\times S$. Furthermore, under the assumption that $P$ has a particular topological characteristic, we prove the existence of a measure $\mu_P$ on $P$, enabling the representation of any symplectic form on $P\times S$ as the sum of $\omega_P$ and an integral of $\mu_P$ over $S$.

The kaon condensation model serves as a substantial Nambu-Goldstone boson generation model. However, this model is challenged by the fact that the kaon's mass does not decrease sufficiently with increasing density in neutron stars. We propose an alternative idea where the generation of the massive Nambu-Goldstone boson is linked to the occurrence of a charged pion condensation at high density within neutron stars. This concept is examined using a linear sigma model, and we analyze the conditions under which a charged pion condensation emerges at the onset, in relation to the interaction between pions and mesons within dense matter. By applying a chiral limit, we are able to compare our results to those obtained from the kaon condensation model and identify key differences in their behavior.

Recent studies suggest that using counterfactual data can facilitate machine learning models in achieving both better robustness and generalization performance. Nonetheless, counterfactual generation methods generally produce diverse counterfactuals, making it challenging for models to distinguish true from false data. To address this issue, a new method called DISCO is proposed, which generates counterfactuals in a single-space setting to facilitate the model's ability to differentiate them from original data. According to the evaluation, using counterfactual data generated by DISCO in the training process leads to a significant enhancement in model performance on both robustness and generalization metrics. Moreover, the proposed method is a one-time cost, as the counterfactual generation model can be reused for various tasks. The efficacy of DISCO is demonstrated across four different datasets, four machine learning models, and three evaluation tasks, and the underlying mechanism is illustrated through an abstract counterfactual dataset. The associated code is openly available on GitHub.

The synthesis of epitaxial materials on graphene substrates, which has a non-uniform surface due to spontaneous domain formation, presents a scientific challenge. Using density functional theory, we investigated the growth of three materials - iron, cobalt, and copper - on a graphene substrate and found that different growth temperatures significantly influence the formation of domains. Notably, below 600 K, all three materials form large domains with a rotated lattice in comparison to the graphite lattice. However, above this temperature, the cobalt and iron materials form small domains with the graphite lattice, whereas the copper material forms small domains with a rotated lattice. Our results suggest that the growth temperature can be used to control the lattice orientation of epitaxial domains in materials grown on graphene and also provide a theoretical explanation for previous experimental observations. Furthermore, our study indicates that the spin polarized nature of cobalt and iron will depend on the lattice orientation, offering a new pathway for designing magnetic materials grown on graphene.

We establish new rank bounds for codes possessing a $ \Z_3 \Z_9$-linear structure, thereby improving upon previous records. Specifically, for an code designated as $C$, having a $ \Z_3 \Z_9$-linear property, we demonstrate that the rank of $C$ is capped at $ \rank(C) \leq \frac{3}{2} \dim_{\Z_3}(C) + \dim_{\Z_9}(C)$, along with an equivalent formulation. This achievement is particularly significant because the prior limitation was both loose and difficult to apply, and codes that violate our current restriction would allow us to draw conclusions about their construction. Moreover, our result includes a subclass of $ \Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes where the rank is limited to $ \rank(C) \leq \frac{3}{2} \dim_{\Z_3}(C) + \dim_{\Z_9}(C) \leq 4$, which represents the most stringent rank criterion established to date for codes within this category.

Selectively labeling data for machine learning models that handle multi-label classification can be a challenging task. Human annotators typically assign all relevant labels to a piece of data, but this process is labor-intensive and costly. To streamline this process, we've developed a technique called S2M, which uses a model to filter out unnecessary labels after an initial random sampling step. To enhance the effectiveness of this approach, we've explored incorporating a priority list of labels and a similarity-based approach to reduce annotation costs further. Experimental results show that our S2M technique outperforms alternative methods of obtaining multi-label data, achieving a 12% increase in accuracy when using a limited set of annotations. Furthermore, our technique is versatile and can be applied to various machine learning tasks, including text and image classification.

We introduce the concept of weak naturality, extending the idea of natural transformation to a more general level, incorporating components with an associated natural isomorphism. Notably, this concept enables the creation of natural transformations between functors that are not initially defined for the same collection of objects. Subsequently, we apply this expanded framework to demonstrate the existence of a weak natural transformation. The purpose of this demonstration is to illustrate the existence of a natural transformation of a specific type, which arises from an adjunction. The adjunction in question, denoted as $F\dashv U$, extends the Functor-Universal property to include objects for which there is an isomorphism, as opposed to an equivalence. Ultimately, this is utilized to provide an interpretation of the functor $UF \simeq F$ through a weak natural transformation.

The Magnetic Field Alignment by Turbulence (MAD) model has been developed to explain the alignment of magnetic fields in turbulent environments and has been successfully applied to the analysis of relativistic jets. However, the efficacy of the MAD model is indirectly affected by the rate of electron heating, which can compromise its ability to match gamma-ray observations above 1 GeV. By incorporating an electron cooling mechanism, the MAD model can be modified to improve consistency with these findings. Using this updated approach, we reconcile the model with the help of an external heating source and demonstrate that it aligns with the findings from Markovic et al. Furthermore, we show that the addition of an electron cooling mechanism aligns the model with a degree of sensitivity that is $10^2-10^3$ times greater than without it, and that the effectiveness of the MAD model in this form is largely independent of the strength of the aligned magnetic fields, supported by a mapping of the parameter space that can be explored observationally.

Deep neural networks have made significant advancements in detecting cardiac abnormalities from sound recordings with a high degree of accuracy. However, real-world data is often contaminated with background noise which can lead to misleading diagnoses. Our innovative solution applies a single-layer convolutional neural network to reduce noise within heart sound recordings prior to analysis. We tested this approach using the PhysioNet 2014 challenge data and found it effective in identifying cardiac abnormalities, outperforming conventional noise-reduction techniques. Our algorithm achieves superior results in both clean and noisy data scenarios, as validated by specialists through clinical evaluations.

MHealth applications on wearable devices are subject to wearable activity recognition errors due to hardware limitations, model size constraints, and high training costs. To overcome these challenges, a new framework called FedHealth has been developed to efficiently train and develop wearable activity recognition applications. FedHealth's innovative feature enables the secure private aggregation of data across devices, significantly enhancing the accuracy of these applications compared to existing methods. The results of the research, conducted on 12 public datasets for activity recognition, reveal that FedHealth achieves superior performance and accuracy compared to leading approaches, successfully bridging the performance gap between centralised and federated learning models. The findings of the research also reveal that FedHealth successfully overcomes data heterogeneity, resulting in a 23.67% improvement in the accuracy of activity recognition. The code for FedHealth is available online at: https://github.com/Hamidreza-H/FedHealth.

The current state of portfolio management strategy optimization is characterized by a lack of uniform framework, resulting in isolated studies. This paper aims to address this limitation by developing a universal framework based on utility and multi-objective optimization. We utilize this framework to explore various optimization approaches, leveraging a sophisticated agent-based model that incorporates risk-management behaviors from Chinese individual investors. By employing a multi-objective genetic algorithm, our study delivers a comprehensive understanding of optimal portfolio management strategies across diverse risk-preference profiles. Furthermore, we investigate multiple scenario-based policies utilizing the developed framework, obtaining tangible policy implications for financial institutions seeking to manage investment products. Ultimately, this research provides a methodology for creating policy-friendly risk-management solutions, enabling financial institutions to create tailored products that minimize risk and maximize returns for their clients.

The recruitment industry faces significant challenges in managing interviews and panel creation, as well as panel recruitment. To address this, we develop an innovative integer programming model that integrates multiple components, including a linear ordering problem to handle interviews with multiple panels, and incorporates various constraints to ensure feasibility. We also create a sophisticated dynamic programming solution to solve the integrated problem, which has a simplified form compared to existing methods. Through extensive experiments using real-world data, we find that our approach outperforms current algorithms and solves problems that were previously unsolvable. Furthermore, our results show that the optimal solution to the integrated problem can be obtained in a significantly shorter time compared to solving each component separately.

This study investigates the value of an optimal payoff in a setting where a diffusion affects the underlying process and path degradation occurs, using the solutions to forward and backward stochastic differential equations as a framework. We first establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions to extended backward stochastic differential equations, and then determine the optimal payoff in the presence of path degradation and a underlying diffusion. A comparison between the optimal payoffs in the diffusive and non-diffusive cases reveals that the presence of the diffusion does not necessarily affect the value of the optimal payoff, although it may impact the strategy for obtaining this value.

The ATLAS and CMS experiments at the CERN Large Hadron Collider have conducted thorough searches for the process of leptoquark pair production, specifically focusing on the $t\bar{t}R$ process via leptoquarks of type $SU(2)_L^{1/3}$ to aid in identifying the characteristics of a 1.4 TeV leptoquark named $R$. To effectively utilize this signal, it's crucial that the decay of leptoquark pairs into top quarks and leptons occurs in a way that the final products appear as top quark antitop quark pairs in conjunction with a vector boson or a Higgs boson. Moreover, to consider this signal, it's necessary to either include a charge asymmetry in the leptoquark pair production process or account for a specific range of leptoquark masses where asymmetry becomes prominent.

Using spectral observations from the VLT, we studied the properties of extremely compact, dusty galaxies in the early universe. By analyzing the spectra of these galaxies, we identified a key feature - a strong emission from a specific ion, which can be produced by either low-density gas in the surroundings of these galaxies or by their own internal winds. We compared the intensities of this emission to different spectral lines and found that the most likely explanation is a dense gas surrounding these galaxies, rather than the galaxies' own wind. We also used computational simulations to better understand these findings and found that the observed properties of these galaxies are consistent with a gas surrounding them, which is being compressed by the intense radiation emitted by the galaxies. We plan to continue this research by studying more of these galaxies and their surrounding environments.

Consider a Cayley graph based on the Hamming distance for a given set of errors and a specific distance. Let's denote the Cayley graph as G_N(d,p) and examine the largest intersection of two metric balls within G_N(d,p). Our goal is to determine the size of this intersection, which we'll refer to as beta_1 in G_N(d,p). To do this, we need to find the minimum value of beta_1 for a given set of errors epsilon and a specific distance k, which we can then use to determine beta_1 for any epsilon and k. For binary codes with a distance of at least 2d+1 and a maximum probability of p< 1/2, we can achieve an accurate approximation of beta_1. For binary codes with a distance of at least 2d and a maximum probability of p< 1/2, we can also determine the exact value of beta_1 for erasure codes with a maximum number of errors up to k.

The accuracy of approximate analytic expressions for the bias in Pulsar Timing Anomaly (PTA) experiments was compared to other methods. To achieve this, the original research was extended by numerically investigating the precision of these expressions under various conditions, incorporating simulated PTA data generated using the PULSAR TIMING MODEL. The results showed that the approximate analytic expressions' accuracy varies significantly, with a maximum absolute error of up to 5.08 minutes in some cases. The approximately analytic expressions' precision proves to be directly correlated with the standard deviation of the PTA's timing residuals. Furthermore, the findings indicated that the precision of these expressions can be influenced by the PTA, but the impact of this effect is found to be negligible in the majority of PTA cases. The research also demonstrated that the precision of these expressions exhibits a near-linear relationship with the PTA's timing residual standard deviation, with a 1-e standard deviation model of $\sigma \approx 5.1\,\left(\frac{\sigma_{\gamma}}{1\,{\rm day}^{1/2}}\right)\,{\rm day}$. The approximately analytic expressions' limited accuracy suggests that their direct application may lead to suboptimal solutions in PTA experiments. The research further suggests that more precise methods, such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo, may yield more accurate results in PTA data processing.

We investigate the ASEP model with two distinct populations of particles, where the injection and ejection processes apply only to distinguished particles. Specifically, we examine how a single distinguished particle, initially at a specific site, moves through the system over time. Our main finding shows that the velocity of this second-class particle follows a specific distribution, which we can determine for any initial configuration of the surrounding population. Our approach involves creating a marked bond directed random walk, which we can solve by developing a new algorithm that efficiently tracks the direction of the walk. By combining the mark on the walk with the Burylinski measure, we obtain the desired velocity distribution. Our results can be interpreted through the perspective of the marked BD RW's inverse process.

When analyzing epidemiological data, modeling the spread of diseases involves creating and fitting mathematical models to time-series data, typically using parameter estimation techniques. However, fitting random field models to spatial data or structural dynamic models to temporal data may not guarantee feasible solutions due to the presence of non-linear constraints, causing issues with the project. This paper addresses this challenge by presenting a method to incorporate biological feasibility into model fitting, using a combination of constraint-based techniques and optimization algorithms. The approach is applied to a model of city-scale influenza spread, resulting in fitted parameters that not only accurately match data but also yield a solution that makes sense in the context of the model.

Researchers have long used various approximations to analyze the dynamics of atom-molecule interactions under angular dispersion, despite these approximations falling short in accurately capturing the underlying physics. In a breakthrough study, we have developed an enhanced non-rigid pendulum model that seamlessly integrates the effects of atomic collisions, momentum distributions, and two-body chemistry, all while maintaining a direct analogy to the original pendulum model. By applying this model to a specific scenario - a one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate undergoing Ramsey folding - we have observed the emergence of chemistry-driven dynamics, atom-molecule phase modulation, and eventual breakdown of the condensate, all of which could be successfully replicated with the non-rigid pendulum model. Furthermore, we have successfully mapped the onset of instability to a simple criterion, demonstrating how the effective model reduces the complexity of real-system dynamics while retaining invaluable insights.

As interest in DNA data storage continues to grow, managing system updates has become a pressing issue. This study examines the impact of primer pair design on storage partition management and presents an innovative approach to dynamically create and update primer pairs. By generating optimal primer pairs based on available DNA sequences in the data bank, this method significantly reduces the need for fixed storage partitions. It also offers a strategy to convert old genotypes to new ones, facilitating widespread adoption of the system. Furthermore, this technique enables the creation of universal primer pairs that can be used with various DNA encodings, thus enabling the use of encoded data across different platforms.

The complex task of accurately mapping riverbed geometry using acoustic Doppler current profilers is costly and time-consuming. To streamline and enhance the efficiency of this process, the principal component geostatistical approach (PCGA) can be utilized to quickly estimate riverbed bathymetry from flow velocity measurements. This study leverages high-resolution models to comprehend the underlying physics and enhances the PCGA framework by incorporating prior information about the riverbed geometry. The improved PCGA method was then applied to a real-world data set from the Snake River, with results showing that it can accurately model the nonlinear relationships between flow velocity and bathymetry, and effectively incorporates prior information to constrain its estimates. Furthermore, the PCGA approach was found to outperform the current state-of-the-art geostatistical approach in terms of estimation accuracy, with a particular advantage in estimating deeper water depths.

Recreating detailed images of real-world scenes requires constructing High Dynamic Range (HDR) images from multiple low-density photos taken at different exposure levels.  Currently available automatic exposure setting selection (AESS) methods in digital cameras fail to effectively handle this problem.  As a result, common AESS algorithms are being explored to enhance HDR image construction.  In this research, a new dataset is introduced to facilitate the assessment of existing AESS algorithms and guide their improvement for capturing optimal images for HDR creation.  A unique evaluation framework is subsequently established to determine how various AESS algorithms interact with the new dataset and enhance the quality of HDR images.  The results show that certain AESS algorithms are more suitable for creating HDR images with the proposed dataset, and HRD image construction can be refined by adjusting exposure settings.  The research findings also reveal that the best AESS algorithms already available can be further improved, and the proposed approach can enhance the quality of HDR images by capturing underexposed details in previously inaccessible scenes.  The newly introduced dataset and methodology for assessing AESS algorithms are available online at: https://ghdrdataset.github.io/.

Identifying and filling gaps in the theory and practice of deep learning methods that account for causality is a pressing challenge. A burgeoning field, causal deep learning relies on increasingly sophisticated techniques to handle ever more complex data. As a result of this diversity, it has become increasingly difficult for both new and established researchers to navigate the field. This paper addresses this difficulty by categorizing modern causal deep learning methods along dimensions of performance, interpretability, and reliability, and by outlining potential areas for future work. This is achieved by examining and organizing the various approaches through the lens of how data is handled, by exploring the underlying mathematics, and by reviewing the applications in prominent fields such as computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning. By synthesizing the numerous perspectives, this paper provides a clear framework for understanding the causal deep learning landscape and highlights promising directions for further investigation.

The Madsen-Weiss theorem states that the space of maps from the universal cover of the surface of a torus to the tree of hyperbolic planes is topologically stable under certain constraints, and this fact can be used to prove the 3-dimensional hyperbolic Thurston's conjecture for certain types of 3-manifolds. Initially proven by Peterlandera, the theorem's connection to hyperbolic geometry was unknown. Recently, the theorem was re-proven by the current authors using the ideas of the recent proof of the 3-dimensional hyperbolic Thurston's conjecture by the Agol-Bowden-Neumann-Sageev team. The purpose of this new proof is to illustrate how the application of the 3-dimensional hyperbolic Thurston's conjecture can be expanded to include spaces of maps from the universal cover of a hyperbolic surface to the tree of hyperbolic planes, and to provide a detailed explanation of the method for achieving this extension.

This study develops a new BDDC preconditioner for a wide range of linear systems resulting from the discretization of mixed form, second-order elliptic partial differential equations. The proposed approach creates a coarse-level problem and distributes the local solutions in accordance with the underlying subdomains. We examine the performance of the suggested BDDC algorithm and compare it to other prominent domain decomposition methods. Our in-depth analysis of the BDDC algorithm is carried out under a diverse set of assumptions, involving non-uniform subdomains of varying numbers of elements. Our research finds that the proposed method consistently delivers high levels of solution accuracy and efficient computational times. In particular, we demonstrate that the proposed BDDC algorithm achieves solution precisions of 10-100 times better than those attained through traditional non-overlapping domain decomposition methods. Furthermore, our study reveals that the proposed BDDC algorithm can solve large problems of up to 500,000 unknowns on a single desktop computer within a day.

We examine the spread of a diffusion process on a network that is characterized by both correlations and variations in connectivity. Contrary to common assumptions, the network is modeled as having non-polarized connections, leading to a focus on the impact of diffusion over time. We find that the process's spread can be described by a generalized linear equation, whose characteristics are determined by the network's properties. We apply this approach to the study of a specific diffusion process, where the process's speed is slowed by the presence of less connected nodes, which can be identified through an inverse linear reconstruction method. We further find that the speed of the diffusion process exhibits robustness across different time frames, both in its linearity and a non-monotonic relationship with the degree of connectivity. We analyze various correlated configurations to determine which ones result in the diffusion process's speed becoming speed-limiting, either partially (tangential to a line) or completely (a parabola). We propose a new statistical method to categorize the outcomes based on their visual representation, and we demonstrate the applicability of this approach to the analysis of empirical data networks, including a renowned scientific collaboration network and Internet map data.

Researchers studying nonlinear optics in loop resonators found that CPD was significantly stronger than SPM in identical counterpropagating modes. To demonstrate, a Mach-Zehnder interferometer with a loop was built, where light passing through could exhibit nonlinear effects in both identical and opposite counterpropagating modes. By varying the input powers, it was shown that the CPD was at least 100 times greater than the SPM in the same counterpropagating modes. Furthermore, when the same counterpropagating modes were identical, the SPM and CPD showed the same strength. This finding, confirmed through numerical simulation, highlights the importance of considering loop resonators as a whole, rather than individual arms, when nonlinear effects are present.

This study creates a deep learning model that improves upon existing super-resolution GANs by incorporating multiscale information. By feeding the network multiple resolution data, we achieve significant performance enhancements, as demonstrated in results showing improved $e^-$ flux enhancement and reduced momentum compensation at super-resolution scales compared to traditional GANs. When applied to turbulent flow simulations, varying the Reynolds number based on this improved model reveals intriguing results. For Reynolds numbers between 550 and 1700, the model accurately predicts near-wall slope values when training at a 'target' Reynolds number, showing the network's ability to learn from a single training data set for multiple Reynolds numbers. However, at a Reynolds number of 5500, the model's near-wall slope predictions fail, as it struggles to capture fully developed turbulence.

We propose a new evaluation method for reinforcement learning algorithms by introducing a controlled sequence of curriculum designs. This approach allows us to assess an agent's ability to adapt to varying levels of task difficulty and relatedness. We investigate multiple curriculum structures, both manually created and automatically generated based on the return distribution, and demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in comparing different reinforcement learning algorithms. Our results show that agents perform better in the controlled curriculum experiment than in standard setting, and the performance under changing curricula reflects the true capabilities of the algorithms, masking some differences visible in traditional evaluations. We further find that the ability of an agent to adapt to changing curricula is a more challenging problem than learning from scratch, and our evaluation framework can be used to determine the optimal curriculum structure and to explore relationships between curriculum design and agent performance.

To better understand complex processes, it's often necessary to analyze multiple data sets from different points in time. Conformance checking helps achieve this understanding by examining how observed data deviates from expected process models. Since processes typically evolve over time, it's essential to have a method to identify changes in process behavior through time. Our approach, known as multi-period conformance checking, uses DCR graphs to determine differences in process behavior at various points in time. DCR graphs distinguish themselves from other conformance checking methods that compare data sets from different time periods by also highlighting the significance of observed discrepancies. Our research introduces a new approach to multi-period conformance checking and presents two variants of the DCR graph, each addressing a distinct aspect of process change. Furthermore, we develop algorithms to compute these DCR graphs and demonstrate their effectiveness in real-world scenarios.

Barry Mazur and Richard Taylor have shown that the moduli space of certain types of hypersurface structures on a variety does not have a higher-dimensional component when viewed from a geometric or Hodge-theoretic perspective. This result can be reinterpreted to demonstrate that under specific assumptions, the image of the Siegel modular form attached to a variety within a particular space of modular forms does not occupy a higher-dimensional subspace when considered using both geometric and Hodge-theoretic approaches.

Using data from the DEEP2 observation program, we studied the relationship between galaxy color based on near-ultraviolet and optical light and the mass of galaxies within flat regions of space. Our research discovered a notable shift in color, indicating a transition to older stellar populations among galaxies with masses exceeding 1.5 times 10 to the power of 10.5 solar masses. This transformation occurs over a wide range of environments, evident despite variations in local density. Furthermore, we found that the transition becomes more defined at greater distances from the center of galaxies, specifically within galaxy clusters at redshift two. The observed shift in color is consistent with a previous finding, but the cause remains a subject of debate.

Transfer learning across languages has seen considerable growth due to reduced modeling needs, allowing the use of existing resources to train on one language and applying it to another. When using multilingual models, it's possible to leverage pre-trained weights to classify the target language's sentiment, despite potential limitations in understanding the target language's semantics. To enhance effectiveness, it's proposed to fine-tune the target language's text generation capabilities before utilizing it to enhance sentiment classification. In assessing this approach for Spanish using an English-based BERT, it was found that it yields a 10% improvement in accuracy compared to directly applying the English BERT. Furthermore, fine-tuning the multilingual XLM-R base model resulted in an even greater achievement, with an 18% improved accuracy in understanding Spanish sentiment.

Resource allocation during the COVID-19 pandemic is highly challenging, with limited healthcare resources needing to be allocated efficiently to varying numbers of patients in need. Early intervention is critical for preventing the collapse of the healthcare system, and this study aims to contribute to this effort by presenting a novel machine learning approach that can be used to prioritize patients. In order to prioritize patients fairly and effectively, this study proposes the use of multi-metric decision-making methods, incorporating clinical characteristics that influence the probability of a patient's recovery as well as the likelihood of the patient defaulting on treatment. The study uses the Technique for Order Performance by Optimizing with Maximal Disappointment Principle to establish a priority order for patients, and develops a feature selection method to simplify the model while maintaining high accuracy. The study's framework is tested on four different datasets of Chinese patients with COVID-19, and the results show that it is effective in prioritizing patients fairly and accurately, with the ability to identify vulnerable patients who may require more urgent attention. The study's priority-scheduling framework can be used by healthcare policymakers to develop more targeted and effective strategies for allocating limited resources to varying numbers of patients in need.

The classical universal bundle functor $E$ maps simplicial groups to simplicial groups with the property that for any simplicial group $G$, $E(G)$ is a simplicial group acting on $G$ through an action that is natural in $G$. This concept can be generalized to any monadic over category, resulting in a concept of universal bundle functors that generates the underlying functors of the monad. This process is demonstrated by creating a universal bundle functor for the monad defined on simplicial groups that produces groups. The resulting functor is equivalent to the classical universal bundle functor, meaning that for any simplicial group $G$, the image of $G$ under this functor is a group acting on $G$, showing that the standard universal bundle functor is functorially self-aware within the category of simplicial groups.

To mitigate the optimization challenges posed by the large number of negative proposals in Visual Relationship Detection, we introduce Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling, a technique that reduces the number of negative proposals through strategic sampling. Unlike existing approaches that focus solely on balancing positive proposals, our method also balances the distribution of negative proposals by prioritizing difficult negatives. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BNPS in improving model performance and efficiency by applying it to three VRD datasets. Our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art approach, Adaptive Negative Proposal Sampling, in model performance on VRC-TS-VRD and VRC-12-VRD, while ADAS is more efficient on VRC-VRD. Notably, BNPS enhances the efficiency of state-of-the-art VRD models by 23% on VRC-VRD and 22% on VRC-TS-VRD without model pretraining.

The merger of galaxies provides a mechanism for mass transfer, potentially leading to
the creation of grand-design spiral arms and influencing galaxy evolution. Accretion
streams from mergers typically dissipate quickly; however, some streams might survive
long enough to impact nearby star-forming gas and contribute to the formation of warps,
bars, and tidal disks. We present the discovery of a massive accretion stream, with a
mass of 7 x 10 to the power 8 solar masses, extending from the central bulge of the
early-type galaxy NGC 4552. This stream has an unusually high surface brightness
and consists of blue, young stars along with various elements of tidal debris. NGC
4552 is the first detected galaxy hosting a visible accretion stream and offers a
unique opportunity to study the effects of minor mergers on galaxy evolution. We
estimate the accretion stream's properties, including its age, which is approximately
one billion years, and propose that its formation triggered the formation of the
tidal tail and contributed to the flattening of the galaxy's central bulge.

A highly intense geomagnetic storm hit Earth on November 7th, 2004, reaching a high strength of 9 on the Kp scale, with widespread power outages and communication disruptions in Asia. Despite its extreme power, researchers found the event's effects on the upper atmosphere were surprisingly mild, with temperatures and winds showing little change from pre-storm levels. Additionally, scientists detected a unusual phenomenon called quasi-standstill flow region, not observed during previous geomagnetic storms, and lasting for nearly three days in the equatorial region of the mesosphere.

This paper examines the possible explanations for KIC 9267654's unique rotation profile, using both spectroscopic and photometric data. We first re-examine the evidence for KIC 9267654's rapid core rotation and slow outer layers, considering various factors that could contribute to its observed profile. We then test three scenarios using numerical simulations in STARSPIN. The first model involves a merger event leading to the formation of a rapidly rotating core, while the second and third models assess the effects of external gravitational interactions and mass loss, respectively. Our analysis shows that while these events leave identifiable marks on the star's rotation profile, they generally result in a different pattern - specifically, a rapid inner layer and a slower core. Consequently, we are unable to rule out any of these scenarios with the data currently available.

The rapid dissemination of news on social media platforms has created issues with the spread of false information. To combat this, various approaches have been proposed for detecting the origin of news, including utilizing graph-based techniques. In the current study, we introduce a novel method called MetaFEND that leverages a graph neural network to create a distinction between genuine and fabricated news. We then conduct extensive experiments using the Google Fact Check Challenge dataset, which includes an in-depth analysis of the effects of different dataset splits and a comparison with leading detection methods. The results show that MetaFEND yields a detection accuracy of 89% for the entire dataset, surpassing the current state-of-the-art by a 4% margin. Additionally, we carry out a feature importance analysis to determine the aspects that MetaFEND considers when distinguishing between true and false news. The code for MetaFEND is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ali Hosseini MetaFEND.

This paper investigates a one-dimensional transport equation with periodic boundary conditions, where solutions can be rapidly displaced due to the influence of a nonlocal flux function that causes decay, no dissipation, and odd initial data. We find that the solution's breakdown occurs within a finite time period, not requiring any smoothness, and its subsequent behavior can be described as it becomes singular and eventually converges to a steady state. We also determine that the shape of the solution remains unchanged and becomes determined by a unique set of parameters within a short-term period. Our study establishes that a solution's short-term behavior is closely linked to the characteristics of its initial data, in contrast to a long-term behavior that is influenced by the global smoothness of the solution. We achieve these results by utilizing the method of characteristics, the nonlocal flux function's properties, and the solution's convergence to a singular steady state, in addition to applying the method of singular limit to analyze the equation's version with a small interface.

Quaternary Golay complementary array pairs in three dimensions are a highly sought-after concept due to their vast applications, however, despite extensive research, no feasible solution has been discovered. This paper delves into the fundamentals of quaternary Golay complementary array pairs and provides a more in-depth analysis of their construction process. Additionally, the paper investigates the possible designs of GCAAs in four dimensions and identifies specific parameters that can facilitate successful implementation.

Researchers are seeking to create a versatile silicon-based quantum processor with a long-range, directional coupling between spin and microwave fields. To achieve this goal, they must carefully design the placement of dopants to control the exchange interaction between adjacent spin sites. By modeling substitutional group V dopants in silicon, scientists found that the exchange interaction can be either facilitated or hindered along specific directions, and that it could be varied significantly across different atomic layers. Furthermore, by substituting silicon atoms with germanium, the exchange interaction was observed to extend over a longer range, and with a more uniform magnitude, making germanium a promising substitute for silicon in quantum processors.

We introduce a novel approach that enables the recovery of a system's underlying structure from observations of its dynamic behavior through probabilistic inference. This method is applicable to various systems and is demonstrated using both linear and nonlinear examples. In addition, we show that effective recovery is achievable even with incomplete data and multiple system instances. A key aspect of our approach is the utilization of time series observations to recover the underlying structure of a new system instance, which can be costly to create through traditional means. This technique leverages observations of a related system to this new instance, which is referred to as the companion system. The accuracy of our approach is validated through the application of Monte Carlo methods to diverse systems, including both linear and nonlinear examples. Furthermore, we show that the proposed technique can be used to develop a new system instance from a companion system with incomplete data.

We introduce a concept called ``partially compatible families of subgroups'' of a given symmetry group, applying this idea to Weyl groups, braid groups, and symmetric groups. Utilizing this framework, we develop "extension functors" which extend functors defined for a subfamily to the entire family. We demonstrate how these extensions enable us to define functors for graded polynomial rings, thereby connecting them to homotopy theory via the concept of stable homotopy types. We show that these functors result in partially compatible families of subgroups within the homotopy group $\pi_1(SO(3++))$, ultimately leading to an interpretation of this homotopy group through the lens of symmetric monoidal categories.

Medical imaging region-of-interest (ROI) segmentation is a time-consuming and manual process, which can be automated using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). While CNNs are effective for entire-image segmentation, their application to specific ROI segmentation poses a significant challenge. Our research focuses on extracting specific regions from medical images using a U-Net architecture, with the goal of reducing computation for those regions. We achieved this by implementing an attention mechanism and designing a U-Net architecture with focused extraction. Our attention U-Net architecture significantly decreased computation needs, with application to liver segmentation from MRI images. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ghimelf/Attention_U_Net.

In GP2, we overhauled the fundamental data structure, Array, resulting in a new data frame called BigArray. This revamped structure, with a block-based memory allocation system, yielded a significant speedup in our graph processing test suite, with improvements ranging from 2.5 times to 11 times faster than the original Array implementation. BigArray's optimized memory management, coupled with a revised memory pooling policy, enabled us to achieve remarkable performance gains, as well as the ability to efficiently handle large arrays on memory-constrained devices.

A novel, comprehensive deep learning framework for extractive automatic summarization has been introduced. This framework addresses both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks, seamlessly integrating them to achieve an optimized solution for supervised summarization. Initially, a unique unsupervised model is developed to obtain relevant semantic information from text data. This is followed by fine-tuning the same model to achieve a supervised feature extraction approach. To enhance performance, a bridge module is introduced to adapt the unsupervised model for supervised data. The proposed framework's effectiveness has been demonstrated through improved results on the CNN/Daily Mail data set, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

We develop an infinite family of topological graphs, labeled $\Theta_k$, alongside an infinite family of Ramsey graphs, labeled as $\Phi_k$. Both $\Theta_k$ and $\Phi_k$ possess distinct characteristics and exhibit both high growth and a small automorphism group. Specifically, for a natural number $d$, we demonstrate the existence of an infinite family of graphs with $k$-ary branching at each vertex, large jump ratio $d$, unbounded diameter, and a finite automorphism group. This expands upon a previous result from 2012, where only branchings with a constant jump ratio were explored.

The development of efficient algorithms for group Lasso has been a significant area of study, as it facilitates variable selection in the presence of continuous or categorical data. Building on the foundational work of initial group Lasso implementations, the GGL algorithm has been created to tackle this challenge and has been shown to offer a $O(p)$ time complexity, representing a notable improvement over its predecessors. In particular, the GGL algorithm has been specifically designed to accommodate the unique requirements of nonlinear models represented through generalized linear mixed effects equations. Furthermore, the algorithm is distinguished by its utilization of an augmented Lagrangian method, a choice that is supported by a theoretical examination demonstrating the convergence of the algorithm. In addition, the algorithm is coupled with an initial strategy that involves sorting the grouped coefficients, and this approach has been found to contribute to its computational efficiency. In order to validate the performance of the GGL algorithm, it has been subject to an extensive set of simulations, with results showing that it compares favorably to the Group Lasso using the proximal gradient algorithm along with the LARS algorithm.

Recent advances in natural language processing have seen models pre-trained on knowledge graphs outperform those pre-trained on text-based data for question-answering tasks. Our research builds on pre-training models in the style of TSP to investigate the longevity of knowledge-based representations and their suitability for fine-tuning on question-answering workloads.
